title: Self-Imposed Deadlines
text:
In 2002 Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch reported two studies on whether people who know they procrastinate will bind themselves with deadlines, and whether it works.

The first study took place in an executive education class at MIT. Students had to write three papers during the semester. In one section, the deadlines were fixed and evenly spaced. In another, students could set their own deadlines for each paper, as late as the last day of class, with a grade penalty for missing whatever date they chose. Rationally, there was no reason to set an early deadline: picking the last day kept every option open. Yet most students chose earlier, spaced deadlines, showing they knew they needed help against their own delays. Still, the students with evenly spaced deadlines set by the instructor earned better grades than those who set their own.

The second study tested this more cleanly. Participants were paid to proofread three long texts over three weeks, earning money for each error found and losing money for each day late. One group had evenly spaced deadlines, one set its own, and one had a single deadline at the end. The group with evenly spaced deadlines found the most errors, missed fewer deadlines and earned the most. The end-deadline group did worst, and the self-imposed group fell in between.

People recognized their tendency to procrastinate, but they did not set their deadlines as well as an outsider would.
lesson: If you tend to put things off, break the work into pieces with spaced deadlines, and consider letting someone else set or enforce them. Self-imposed limits help, but outside ones help more.
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA
source: Ariely, D., and Wertenbroch, K. (2002). Procrastination, deadlines, and performance: Self-control by precommitment. Psychological Science, 13(3), 219-224.
